verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The city is under siege and its judge is struck on the cheek (v. 1). But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, too little to be counted among Judah's clans, will produce one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (v. 2). After a time of waiting he will shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, and he shall be great to the ends of the earth (vv. 3-4). And he shall be their peace, ample deliverance against every Assyrian (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a besieged world is a ruler born in a village, whose origins are ancient and whose reign reaches the ends of the earth.

verseByVerse.quote: Now muster your troops, O daughter of troops; siege is laid against us; with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek. But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now muster your troops, O daughter of troops; siege is laid against us; with a rod they strike the judge of Israel on the cheek.

(In the Hebrew Bible this verse is numbered 4:14, as the ESV notes.) The scene is humiliating. The city is under siege (the ESV notes that daughter of troops means the city itself), and the judge of Israel, the king, is struck on the cheek with a rod, the way a slave might be hit. David's throne has come to this.

Christians can hardly read the line without remembering another judge of Israel who was struck on the face: Then they spit in his face and struck him (Matt 26:67), just as Isaiah had foreseen, I gave my back to those who strike (Isa 50:6).

But you, O Bethlehem Ephrathah, who are too little to be among the clans of Judah, from you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days.

This is the great word of the book, and everything in it is surprising.

But you: against the humiliation of verse 1, God sets a promise. O Bethlehem Ephrathah: not Jerusalem, the capital, but a farming village a few miles south, David's home town, so small it was too little to be among the clans of Judah. God's habit is to start in places nobody is watching.

From you shall come forth for me one who is to be ruler in Israel. Note the words for me. This king is God's own choice, for God's own purposes.

Then the line that lifts the promise beyond any ordinary king: whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days. Many in the church, including the Reformed tradition, understand this of the eternal origin of the Son of God, who was in the beginning with God (John 1:1) and is before all things (Col 1:17). Others take it to mean that his family line goes back to ancient times, to David and beyond. The first reading fits the language best: a birth in a village is set beside a going forth from ancient days. The child who would be born in Bethlehem was older than Bethlehem.

Seven hundred years later, when foreign scholars asked where the Christ was to be born, the chief priests answered without hesitation, In Bethlehem of Judea, for so it is written by the prophet (Matt 2:5). Their quotation reads a little differently from Micah's words, calling Bethlehem by no means least, which brings out the point: the village was small, and God's choice made it great. Matthew's version also folds in the promise that this ruler would shepherd my people Israel.

And notice the tragedy in that scene. The scholars knew the verse, quoted it accurately, and stayed in Jerusalem. Knowing the Bible is not the same as going to Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of his brothers shall return to the people of Israel. And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. And they shall dwell secure, for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore he shall give them up until the time when she who is in labor has given birth; then the rest of his brothers shall return to the people of Israel.

Between the promise and its fulfilment lies a long wait. God shall give them up for a time: the exile, and the centuries when no son of David reigned. The waiting is measured by a birth, until the time when she who is in labor has given birth. Isaiah, preaching alongside Micah, had spoken of a virgin who would conceive and bear a son (Isa 7:14).

Then the rest of his brothers shall return. The scattered people of God are gathered again around the newborn king.

And he shall stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, in the majesty of the name of the LORD his God. And they shall dwell secure, for now he shall be great to the ends of the earth.

Look at what this ruler does. He does not exploit; he shall stand and shepherd his flock. Micah has already described leaders who fleeced and devoured the flock (3:1-3). Here at last is a shepherd who feeds it.

He does it in the strength of the LORD, not in his own, and the result is that his people dwell secure. And his reach is not a small kingdom: he shall be great to the ends of the earth. Jesus said, I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep (John 10:11), and after his resurrection sent his people to all nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And he shall be their peace. When the Assyrian comes into our land and treads in our palaces, then we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight princes of men; they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod at its entrances; and he shall deliver us from the Assyrian when he comes into our land and treads within our border.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And he shall be their peace. When the Assyrian comes into our land and treads in our palaces, then we will raise against him seven shepherds and eight princes of men;

And he shall be their peace. Not "he shall bring peace" but he shall be it. Peace is not a policy he arranges; it is a person the people have. Paul writes of Christ, he himself is our peace (Eph 2:14).

The Assyrian was the terror of Micah's own day, and stands here for every hostile power that ever tramples God's people. Against such an enemy God raises seven shepherds and eight princes. Hebrew often counts like this, naming a number and then one more, as Amos did with three transgressions ... and for four (Amos 1:3). The sense is: more than enough. God is never short of deliverers.

they shall shepherd the land of Assyria with the sword, and the land of Nimrod at its entrances; and he shall deliver us from the Assyrian when he comes into our land and treads within our border.

The land of Nimrod is another name for the region of Assyria and Babylon, going back to the mighty hunter whose kingdom began at Babel (Gen 10:8-10). There is grim irony in the wording: the invaders came to shepherd others with the sword, and now they will be shepherded that way themselves.

The promise ends where it must: he shall deliver us. Not the seven shepherds; he.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–15 — Dew, Lion, and the End of False Trusts
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remnant will be like dew from the LORD among the peoples, and also like a lion among the beasts of the forest (vv. 7-9). Then God will cut away everything his people have trusted instead of him: horses and chariots, cities and strongholds, sorceries and fortune-tellers, carved images and pillars and Asherah images (vv. 10-14), and will take vengeance on the disobedient nations (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: God removes his people's false securities, not to leave them defenceless, but to leave them with himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, which delay not for a man nor wait for the children of man. And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep, which, when it goes through, treads down and tears in pieces, and there is none to deliver. Your hand shall be lifted up over your adversaries, and all your enemies shall be cut off.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the remnant of Jacob shall be in the midst of many peoples like dew from the LORD, like showers on the grass, which delay not for a man nor wait for the children of man.

Here is the first picture of God's people living among the nations: like dew from the LORD. Dew appears silently overnight and brings life to dry ground. It does not come because people arrange it; it does not wait for the children of man. So God's people, scattered among the nations, are a quiet, God-given blessing wherever they are.

And the remnant of Jacob shall be among the nations, in the midst of many peoples, like a lion among the beasts of the forest, like a young lion among the flocks of sheep, which, when it goes through, treads down and tears in pieces, and there is none to deliver.

The second picture is the opposite: like a lion. The same people are dew to some and a lion to others. This is a hard image, and it belongs to God's judgment on nations that set themselves against him.

The New Testament says something similar about the gospel: to some it is the fragrance of life, and to others the smell of death. The church's calling is to be dew; but the word we carry is not neutral, and those who refuse it are not left untouched.

Your hand shall be lifted up over your adversaries, and all your enemies shall be cut off.

The outcome is certain. For a small, bullied people in the eighth century BC, this was a promise to hold on to; for the church under pressure it still is.

verseByVerse.quote: And in that day, declares the LORD, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots; and I will cut off the cities of your land and throw down all your strongholds; and I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more tellers of fortunes; and I will cut off your carved images and your pillars from among you, and you shall bow down no more to the work of your hands; and I will root out your Asherah images from among you and destroy your cities. And in anger and wrath I will execute vengeance on the nations that did not obey.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And in that day, declares the LORD, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your chariots;

and I will cut off the cities of your land and throw down all your strongholds;

Now something unexpected. God promises victory, and then he starts destroying his own people's equipment. Four times the phrase falls, I will cut off, and a fifth time he says I will root out.

First the military: horses, chariots, fortified cities and strongholds. These were what Judah had been trusting instead of God, as Micah has already said of Lachish (1:13). A people who are promised that the LORD is their deliverer do not need a chariot corps, and while they have one they will trust it.

and I will cut off sorceries from your hand, and you shall have no more tellers of fortunes;

and I will cut off your carved images and your pillars from among you, and you shall bow down no more to the work of your hands;

and I will root out your Asherah images from among you and destroy your cities.

Next the occult and the idolatrous. Sorceries and tellers of fortunes were attempts to control the future without God. Carved images, pillars and Asherah images were the furniture of Canaanite worship, which Israel had mixed with the worship of the LORD.

Notice the phrase the work of your hands. That is what every idol is, ancient or modern: something we make, and then serve.

It is important to see this as grace. God is not stripping his people bare out of spite. He is removing the things that would fail them, so that they are left holding on to the only One who will not. Scripture says it plainly: God disciplines those he loves (Heb 12:6). Anyone who has watched God dismantle a security they had quietly put in his place will recognise this list.

And in anger and wrath I will execute vengeance on the nations that did not obey.

The chapter closes with the other side of the same coin. God purifies his people and judges the nations that will not listen. Both come from the same holiness, and both are settled by the ruler from Bethlehem, who is at once the shepherd of his flock and the judge of the earth.

5.title: The Ruler from Bethlehem
5.overview:
The city is besieged and Israel's judge is struck on the cheek with a rod (v. 1). But from Bethlehem Ephrathah, too little to be counted among Judah's clans, God will bring forth one who is to be ruler in Israel, whose coming forth is from of old, from ancient days (v. 2). God will give his people up until she who is in labour has given birth, and then the rest of his brothers will return (v. 3). He will stand and shepherd his flock in the strength of the LORD, and they will dwell secure, for he will be great to the ends of the earth (v. 4). He himself will be their peace: when the Assyrian invades, seven shepherds and eight princes will be raised against him, and God's ruler will deliver his people (vv. 5-6).

The remnant of Jacob will be among many peoples like dew from the LORD, and also like a lion among flocks, and their hand will be lifted over their adversaries (vv. 7-9).

In that day God will cut off horses and chariots, cities and strongholds, sorceries and fortune-tellers, carved images, pillars and Asherah images, so that his people bow no more to the work of their hands (vv. 10-14); and he will execute vengeance in anger on the nations that did not obey (v. 15).
5.theology:
God's chosen ruler comes from an overlooked village, and his origin is from ancient days (v. 2; John 1:1; Col 1:17; Matt 2:5-6).

God's promises often involve long waiting, measured out until the appointed birth (v. 3; Isa 7:14).

Christ is the shepherd-king who feeds the flock in God's strength, in contrast to leaders who devour it (v. 4; 3:1-3; John 10:11).

Peace is not an arrangement but a person: he himself is our peace (v. 5; Eph 2:14).

God is never short of deliverers for his people (vv. 5-6).

God's people among the nations are both a life-giving dew and, to those who resist God, a lion (vv. 7-8).

God graciously destroys the false securities of his own people, military, occult and idolatrous, so that they are left trusting him alone (vv. 10-14).
5.examples:
A king slapped on the cheek with a stick.

A village too small to be listed, chosen to produce a ruler.

Scholars who quote the right verse and stay where they are.

A shepherd who feeds the flock instead of eating it.

Seven deliverers, and one more, because God is never short.

Dew that nobody ordered, appearing overnight on dry grass.

God taking away the chariots he had promised to make unnecessary.

How have I wearied you? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old?<sup>7</sup>Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"<sup>8</sup>He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?<sup>9</sup>The voice of the LORD cries to the city— and it is sound wisdom to fear your name: "Hear of the rod and of him who appointed it!<sup>10</sup>Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed?<sup>11</sup>Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales and with a bag of deceitful weights?<sup>12</sup>Your rich men are full of violence; your inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.<sup>13</sup>Therefore I strike you with a grievous blow, making you desolate because of your sins.<sup>14</sup>You shall eat, but not be satisfied, and there shall be hunger within you; you shall put away, but not preserve, and what you preserve I will give to the sword.<sup>15</sup>You shall sow, but not reap; you shall tread olives, but not anoint yourselves with oil; you shall tread grapes, but not drink wine.<sup>16</sup>For you have kept the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their counsels, that I may make you a desolation, and your inhabitants a hissing; so you shall bear the scorn of my people."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–8 — The LORD Has an Indictment
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God calls the mountains to hear his case: O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me! (vv. 1-3). His evidence is his kindness: the exodus, Moses, Aaron and Miriam, and his protection from Balak and Balaam (vv. 4-5). The people ask what offering could possibly satisfy him, even my firstborn (vv. 6-7). The answer is famous: to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God (v. 8).
verseByVerse.theology: God's complaint against his people is not that he has failed them but that they have forgotten his goodness, and what he wants is not a bigger offering but a changed life.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear what the LORD says: Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice. Hear, you mountains, the indictment of the LORD, and you enduring foundations of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against his people, and he will contend with Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear what the LORD says: Arise, plead your case before the mountains, and let the hills hear your voice.

Hear, you mountains, the indictment of the LORD, and you enduring foundations of the earth, for the LORD has an indictment against his people, and he will contend with Israel.

The chapter opens as a courtroom scene, and the jury is the landscape. The mountains and the enduring foundations of the earth are summoned to listen, because they have been there from the beginning and have watched the whole history between God and his people.

The word indictment means a legal case. But notice the tenderness in it: God says he will contend with Israel, his own people. He is not walking away from them; he is arguing with them, which is what you do with someone you refuse to lose.

verseByVerse.quote: "O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me! For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam. O my people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, and what happened from Shittim to Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
"O my people, what have I done to you? How have I wearied you? Answer me!

God opens his case with a question that must have stunned them. Not "how dare you", but what have I done to you? The Judge of all the earth invites his people to state their complaint against him. How have I wearied you? Have I asked too much? Have I been a burden?

People drift from God and rarely say why. If we are honest, the answer to God's question is usually that he has done nothing wrong at all. We simply wanted something else.

For I brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery, and I sent before you Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

His evidence is not a list of their failures but a list of his kindnesses. He brought you up from the land of Egypt and redeemed you from the house of slavery. Redemption means buying someone out of bondage: they were slaves, and he paid to have them out. And he did not leave them leaderless: he gave them Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

O my people, remember what Balak king of Moab devised, and what Balaam the son of Beor answered him, and what happened from Shittim to Gilgal, that you may know the righteous acts of the LORD."

God recalls a rescue they never even saw. Balak king of Moab hired the prophet Balaam to curse Israel, and God turned every curse into a blessing (Num 22-24). Israel was camped in the valley, unaware. Then from Shittim to Gilgal: from their last camp east of the Jordan to their first camp in the promised land (Josh 4:19), God brought them across the river.

These are the righteous acts of the LORD, the things he has done right by them. And this is the order of the Bible: grace first, then obedience. Before God asks anything of his people in verse 8, he reminds them of everything he has done for them in verses 4-5. Christians read the same order in the gospel: Christ has redeemed us, therefore we live for him.

verseByVerse.quote: "With what shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old? Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
"With what shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before God on high? Shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves a year old?

Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, with ten thousands of rivers of oil? Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

Now a worshipper answers, and you can hear the panic rising. What will it take? He starts where the law starts, with burnt offerings and calves a year old, and then the offers get wilder: thousands of rams, ten thousands of rivers of oil (the ESV notes the question may read "Will the LORD accept"). Nobody has rivers of oil. He is bidding against himself.

And then the terrible last offer: Shall I give my firstborn for my transgression? That was not merely rhetorical. King Ahaz, in Micah's own lifetime, burned his son as an offering (2 Kgs 16:3). This is where religion goes when it believes God must be bought: eventually it will pay anything, even a child.

Behind the escalation is an assumption that must be named, because it is still with us: that God is angry and can be appeased if the price is high enough. People still try to buy him with money, with service, with self-punishment.

The Bible's answer to the question with what shall I come before the LORD is ultimately not verse 8 but the cross. God did give a firstborn son for transgression, and it was his own.

verseByVerse.quote: He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the LORD require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?

Here is the verse everyone knows, and it answers the panic of verses 6-7 with calm. He has told you: this is not a secret. God has already said what he wants, in the law and through the prophets, and it was never rivers of oil.

To do justice. Not to admire it, or to have opinions about it, but to do it: pay fair wages, tell the truth in court, leave the poor man his field. Micah has already shown what its absence looks like.

To love kindness. (The ESV notes this may be rendered "steadfast love", the great covenant word for God's loyal, committed love.) And the verb matters: not "to practise kindness" but to love it. God wants people who delight in mercy, not people who ration it out grudgingly.

To walk humbly with your God. Here is the root of the other two. Walk is a whole life, step after step, day after day. Humbly is the opposite of the proud plotters of chapter 2. And with your God: this is companionship, not servitude.

Two mistakes are easy here. The first is to treat this verse as a ladder, as though God were saying: do these three things and you will be acceptable. But remember verses 4-5. God has already redeemed these people from slavery. This is the shape of a rescued life, not the price of rescue. Paul says we are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (Rom 3:24), and none of us has done justice, loved kindness and walked humbly as we should.

The second mistake is to use the first mistake as an excuse, quoting grace and ignoring the verse. Jesus would not allow that. He rebuked religious experts who tithed their garden herbs and neglected the weightier matters of the law: justice and mercy and faithfulness (Matt 23:23).

So hold both. Only Christ has kept this verse perfectly, and he kept it for us. And everyone who belongs to him is being remade into the kind of person it describes.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9–16 — Wicked Scales and Empty Harvests
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God cries to the city about the treasures of wickedness, wicked scales and a bag of deceitful weights, and a population given to violence and lies (vv. 9-12). So he strikes them: they will eat and not be satisfied, sow and not reap, tread olives and grapes and enjoy neither (vv. 13-15). They have kept the statutes of Omri and walked in the ways of Ahab's house, and will bear the scorn of the nations (v. 16).
verseByVerse.theology: Dishonest gain is never blessed, and a people who copy the worst of their history inherit its ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: The voice of the LORD cries to the city— and it is sound wisdom to fear your name: "Hear of the rod and of him who appointed it! Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed? Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales and with a bag of deceitful weights? Your rich men are full of violence; your inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The voice of the LORD cries to the city— and it is sound wisdom to fear your name: "Hear of the rod and of him who appointed it!

God's voice calls to the city, and Micah breaks in to say that it is sound wisdom to fear your name. Fearing God is not superstition; it is realism, and the wisest thing a city can do. (The ESV notes that the meaning of the rest of the verse is uncertain in Hebrew; the sense is a call to hear the rod of judgment and recognise who has appointed it.)

Can I forget any longer the treasures of wickedness in the house of the wicked, and the scant measure that is accursed?

Shall I acquit the man with wicked scales and with a bag of deceitful weights?

Now we learn what God has been watching, and it is startlingly small-scale: the scant measure, wicked scales, a bag of deceitful weights. A merchant carried stone weights in a bag; a dishonest one carried two sets, a heavy stone for buying and a light one for selling. God's law said, You shall have just balances, just weights (Lev 19:36).

God notices the shop counter. Not only wars and injustice in high places, but the short weight, the padded invoice, the hours claimed and not worked. Shall I acquit such a man? The question expects the answer no. (The ESV notes an alternative reading of verse 10, "Are there still treasures".)

Your rich men are full of violence; your inhabitants speak lies, and their tongue is deceitful in their mouth.

From the scales to the tongue. Violence at the top and lying throughout the population; dishonesty in business and dishonesty in speech are the same disease in different organs. (The ESV notes the Hebrew reads "whose".)

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore I strike you with a grievous blow, making you desolate because of your sins. You shall eat, but not be satisfied, and there shall be hunger within you; you shall put away, but not preserve, and what you preserve I will give to the sword. You shall sow, but not reap; you shall tread olives, but not anoint yourselves with oil; you shall tread grapes, but not drink wine. For you have kept the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their counsels, that I may make you a desolation, and your inhabitants a hissing; so you shall bear the scorn of my people."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Therefore I strike you with a grievous blow, making you desolate because of your sins.

You shall eat, but not be satisfied, and there shall be hunger within you; you shall put away, but not preserve, and what you preserve I will give to the sword.

You shall sow, but not reap; you shall tread olives, but not anoint yourselves with oil; you shall tread grapes, but not drink wine.

The judgment is futility. They will work and get nothing from it: eat without being satisfied, store food that they will not keep, sow fields that others will reap, press oil and wine they will never enjoy. This is exactly what God's covenant had warned centuries earlier (Deut 28:38-40).

There is a spiritual principle here that outlives the covenant with Israel. Gain that God does not bless does not satisfy. People can accumulate for years and find at the end that they are still hungry.

For you have kept the statutes of Omri, and all the works of the house of Ahab; and you have walked in their counsels, that I may make you a desolation, and your inhabitants a hissing; so you shall bear the scorn of my people."

The last verse names the pattern they have copied. Omri founded the dynasty of the northern kingdom and did what was evil in the sight of the LORD (1 Kgs 16:25), and his son Ahab with Jezebel made Baal worship the state religion and murdered Naboth for his vineyard. Judah had watched all that, seen the north destroyed for it, and adopted the same policies. (The ESV notes the Hebrew of this verse reads, "For the statutes of Omri are kept".)

Nations, churches and families copy the worst of their own history with remarkable persistence. The chapter ends in scorn, which is where following Omri always ends. And yet the God who brings this indictment is the same God who, one chapter later, delights in steadfast love and casts sins into the depths of the sea.

6.title: What Does the LORD Require of You?
6.overview:
God calls his people to plead their case before the mountains, for the LORD has an indictment against Israel (vv. 1-2). He asks what he has done to them, and how he has wearied them, and answers with his own record: he brought them out of Egypt, redeemed them from slavery and sent Moses, Aaron and Miriam; he turned Balak and Balaam's plans aside, and brought them from Shittim to Gilgal (vv. 3-5).

A worshipper asks what he should bring: burnt offerings, calves, thousands of rams, ten thousands of rivers of oil, even his firstborn for his transgression (vv. 6-7). The answer is that God has already told them what is good: to do justice, to love kindness and to walk humbly with their God (v. 8).

The voice of the LORD cries to the city about the treasures of wickedness, the scant measure, wicked scales and deceitful weights, rich men full of violence and inhabitants who speak lies (vv. 9-12). So God strikes them: they will eat without being satisfied, sow without reaping, tread olives and grapes without oil or wine (vv. 13-15). They have kept the statutes of Omri and the works of the house of Ahab, and will be made a desolation and bear scorn (v. 16).
6.theology:
God argues with his people rather than abandoning them, and calls creation to witness (vv. 1-2).

God's case against us rests on his kindness, not our excuses; grace comes before demand (vv. 3-5).

Religion that tries to buy God will pay any price and never find peace; only God's own gift answers the question "with what shall I come?" (vv. 6-7; Rom 3:24-25).

What God requires is justice done, mercy loved and a humble walk with him — the shape of a redeemed life, not the price of redemption (v. 8; Deut 10:12; Matt 23:23).

God watches the shop counter: short measures and false weights are sins he will not acquit (vv. 10-11; Lev 19:36; Prov 11:1).

Gain God does not bless does not satisfy; futility is itself a judgment (vv. 14-15; Deut 28:38-40).

Copying the worst patterns of our history leads to the same ruin those patterns produced (v. 16; 1 Kgs 16:25-33).
6.examples:
Mountains called into court as witnesses.

God asking his people what he has done wrong.

A worshipper bidding against himself: rams, rivers of oil, a child.

Three plain requirements answering a panic of offers.

Two sets of weights in one merchant's bag.

Olives pressed by men who will never use the oil.

A southern kingdom copying the policies that destroyed the north.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — No One Upright Is Left
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah laments that he is like a man looking for fruit after the harvest: The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind (vv. 1-2). Officials and judges take bribes and weave their schemes together (vv. 3-4). Trust has collapsed so far that a man's enemies are the men of his own house (vv. 5-6). But as for me, I will look to the LORD (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: When society and even family fail, the believer's answer is not despair but waiting on God.

verseByVerse.quote: Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered, as when the grapes have been gleaned: there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fig that my soul desires. The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind; they all lie in wait for blood, and each hunts the other with a net. Their hands are on what is evil, to do it well; the prince and the judge ask for a bribe, and the great man utters the evil desire of his soul; thus they weave it together. The best of them is like a brier, the most upright of them a thorn hedge. The day of your watchmen, of your punishment, has come; now their confusion is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Woe is me! For I have become as when the summer fruit has been gathered, as when the grapes have been gleaned: there is no cluster to eat, no first-ripe fig that my soul desires.

Micah speaks as a hungry man walking through an orchard after the pickers have been through. He wants no first-ripe fig, that early fig which is the best of the season. There is nothing left.

The godly has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among mankind; they all lie in wait for blood, and each hunts the other with a net.

The orchard is his society, and the missing fruit is godly people. The godly has perished: the word covers people who are loyal, kind and faithful. Instead everyone is hunting: each hunts the other with a net, as if human beings were game.

Micah is not making a careful statistical statement; he is a grieving man describing what it feels like to look for one honest person and not find one. Anyone who has watched a community, a workplace or a church go bad knows the feeling.

Their hands are on what is evil, to do it well; the prince and the judge ask for a bribe, and the great man utters the evil desire of his soul; thus they weave it together.

Here is corruption as a craft. Their hands are on evil to do it well: they have become skilful at it. The prince, the judge and the great man work as a team, and thus they weave it together, as three strands are twisted into one rope. Corruption is rarely one person; it is a network, and each strand makes the others stronger.

The best of them is like a brier, the most upright of them a thorn hedge. The day of your watchmen, of your punishment, has come; now their confusion is at hand.

Even the best of them scratches and tears like a brier. And the day the watchmen warned about has arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: Put no trust in a neighbor; have no confidence in a friend; guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms; for the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house. But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Put no trust in a neighbor; have no confidence in a friend; guard the doors of your mouth from her who lies in your arms;

for the son treats the father with contempt, the daughter rises up against her mother, the daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law; a man's enemies are the men of his own house.

When a society rots, it rots inward, until it reaches the last place people expect: home. Do not confide in a neighbor, or a friend, or even the wife who lies in your arms (the ESV notes the Hebrew word is "bosom"). Children despise parents; in-laws turn on each other. A man's enemies are the men of his own house.

Jesus quoted these very words, but he gave them a different setting. He said that his coming would divide households, that a person's enemies will be those of his own household (Matt 10:35-36), because some in a family follow him and others refuse. Micah describes a family breaking apart through sin; Jesus warns that a family may break apart over him. Both are painful, and many Christians know the second first-hand. He does not promise us that our households will be united; he promises that he is worth the cost.

But as for me, I will look to the LORD; I will wait for the God of my salvation; my God will hear me.

This is the hinge of the chapter, and one of the great verses for dark times. Micah has looked at his society and found nothing. So he lifts his eyes.

Three things hold him steady. I will look to the LORD: a deliberate act of attention, away from the mess and toward God. I will wait for the God of my salvation: he does not expect an instant answer, and he does not stop expecting one. My God will hear me: not "may hear", but will.

Notice that this comes after, not instead of, honest lament. The Bible never asks us to pretend things are fine. It asks us to look up while telling the truth about what is down here.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–13 — When I Fall, I Shall Rise
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me (v. 8). The fallen people accept God's discipline because I have sinned against him, and wait for him to plead my cause and bring them out to the light (vv. 9-10). Walls will be rebuilt and the scattered gathered from Assyria to Egypt, though the earth is desolate for its inhabitants' deeds (vv. 11-13).
verseByVerse.theology: A believer who has fallen under God's hand can still be sure of rising, because the God who disciplines is the God who vindicates.

verseByVerse.quote: Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me. I will bear the indignation of the LORD because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication. Then my enemy will see, and shame will cover her who said to me, "Where is the LORD your God?" My eyes will look upon her; now she will be trampled down like the mire of the streets.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Rejoice not over me, O my enemy; when I fall, I shall rise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD will be a light to me.

Now the voice is the voice of God's people, beaten and mocked. And what she says to the gloating enemy is magnificent: when I fall, I shall rise. Not "if" but when. She knows she will fall, and she knows she will not stay down, because rising is not something she does for herself: the LORD will be a light to me.

Proverbs says the same: the righteous falls seven times and rises again (Prov 24:16). The difference between a believer and an unbeliever is not that one falls and the other does not. It is what happens next.

I will bear the indignation of the LORD because I have sinned against him, until he pleads my cause and executes judgment for me. He will bring me out to the light; I shall look upon his vindication.

Here is a remarkably mature confession. She does not protest her innocence: I have sinned against him. She accepts the discipline: I will bear the indignation of the LORD. And at the same time she is certain it will end: until he pleads my cause.

Think about that picture. God is the judge who has sentenced her, and also the advocate who will plead her case. That seems impossible until the cross. Paul asks, Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies, and answers that Christ Jesus is at the right hand of God ... interceding for us (Rom 8:33-34).

Then my enemy will see, and shame will cover her who said to me, "Where is the LORD your God?" My eyes will look upon her; now she will be trampled down like the mire of the streets.

The taunt Where is the LORD your God? is the oldest jeer in the world, and it stings because at the time there is no visible answer. The answer comes later, and it comes from God, not from us.

verseByVerse.quote: A day for the building of your walls! In that day the boundary shall be far extended. In that day they will come to you, from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt to the River, from sea to sea and from mountain to mountain. But the earth will be desolate because of its inhabitants, for the fruit of their deeds.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A day for the building of your walls! In that day the boundary shall be far extended.

After the darkness, a shout: A day for the building of your walls! The ruined city of 3:12 will be rebuilt, and its boundary pushed far out.

In that day they will come to you, from Assyria and the cities of Egypt, and from Egypt to the River, from sea to sea and from mountain to mountain.

Who will come? People from Assyria and Egypt, the two superpowers that had terrorised Israel for centuries, and from as far as the River (the ESV notes this means the Euphrates). The old enemies are now pilgrims, arriving from every direction. This is the same vision as chapter 4: the nations streaming to God's mountain. (The ESV notes that the Hebrew reads "he" where the ESV has they.)

But the earth will be desolate because of its inhabitants, for the fruit of their deeds.

Alongside the ingathering stands the sober fact of judgment. The two run together all through the Bible: the world reaps the fruit of their deeds, and out of that world God gathers a people from every nation.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–20 — Who Is a God Like You?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Micah prays, Shepherd your people with your staff, and God promises marvelous things like the days of the exodus, before which the nations will stand ashamed (vv. 14-17). The book ends in wonder: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression, who delights in steadfast love, treads our iniquities underfoot and casts our sins into the depths of the sea, keeping the oath sworn to Abraham (vv. 18-20).
verseByVerse.theology: The last word of Micah is not judgment but a God whose willingness to forgive has no equal.

verseByVerse.quote: Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock of your inheritance, who dwell alone in a forest in the midst of a garden land; let them graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old. As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt, I will show them marvelous things. The nations shall see and be ashamed of all their might; they shall lay their hands on their mouths; their ears shall be deaf; they shall lick the dust like a serpent, like the crawling things of the earth; they shall come trembling out of their strongholds; they shall turn in dread to the LORD our God, and they shall be in fear of you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shepherd your people with your staff, the flock of your inheritance, who dwell alone in a forest in the midst of a garden land; let them graze in Bashan and Gilead as in the days of old.

Micah prays. After all the corrupt shepherds of chapter 3, he asks the true Shepherd to take the work himself: Shepherd your people with your staff. They are the flock of your inheritance, God's own portion.

The flock is pictured alone in a forest surrounded by a garden land (the ESV notes the Hebrew says "of Carmel", the fertile ridge). They are isolated in scrub while rich pasture lies around them. So he asks for the good pastures of Bashan and Gilead again, the best grazing land Israel had ever held.

As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt, I will show them marvelous things.

God answers the prayer, and his answer reaches back to the exodus: As in the days when you came out of the land of Egypt (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "him"). The God who did those things has not changed, and his people may ask him to act again in character.

The nations shall see and be ashamed of all their might; they shall lay their hands on their mouths; their ears shall be deaf;

they shall lick the dust like a serpent, like the crawling things of the earth; they shall come trembling out of their strongholds; they shall turn in dread to the LORD our God, and they shall be in fear of you.

The proud nations end with their hands over their mouths, out of arguments. They come trembling out of their strongholds, the fortresses they trusted. And the last phrase turns even this toward hope: they shall turn in dread to the LORD our God. They turn to him. Fear of God is the beginning of wisdom, and for some it is the beginning of salvation.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love. He will again have compassion on us; he will tread our iniquities underfoot. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea. You will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity and passing over transgression for the remnant of his inheritance? He does not retain his anger forever, because he delights in steadfast love.

The book ends in wonder. After seven chapters of indictment, Micah looks at the God who has every right to destroy, and asks, Who is a God like you? The answer is nobody, and the reason is not his power but his pardon.

Look at the words. Pardoning iniquity: lifting the guilt off. Passing over transgression: stepping past what he could have stopped to punish. He does not retain his anger forever: he will not nurse a grievance, though he has the best of reasons. And then the reason for all of it: because he delights in steadfast love. God does not forgive reluctantly. Mercy is what he enjoys.

This is the God the whole Bible reveals, and it raises a question Micah could not fully answer: how can a just God pass over transgression without ceasing to be just? The New Testament gives the answer. God put forward Christ as a propitiation by his blood, precisely to show his righteousness while passing over sins (Rom 3:25). Micah's wonder is right, and the cross is where it is explained.

He will again have compassion on us; he will tread our iniquities underfoot. You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea.

Two pictures, and both repay a slow reading. God will tread our iniquities underfoot, crushing them like an enemy. And he will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea (the ESV notes the Hebrew reads "their"). Not into the shallows where they can be fished out; into the depths, where nothing is recovered.

The psalm says he removes our transgressions as far as the east is from the west (Ps 103:12), and God promises in the new covenant, I will remember their sins no more (Heb 8:12). Christians who keep dragging their forgiven sins back up to the surface should notice where God has put them.

You will show faithfulness to Jacob and steadfast love to Abraham, as you have sworn to our fathers from the days of old.

The last verse grounds all this mercy in something outside us: the promise God sworn to our fathers, to Jacob and Abraham, centuries before. Our forgiveness does not rest on our performance but on God's oath.

When Zechariah held his newborn son and prophesied about the coming of Christ, he said God had acted to show the mercy promised to our fathers and to remember his holy covenant, the oath that he swore to our father Abraham (Luke 1:72-73). Micah ends where the gospel begins: an unbreakable promise, a God who delights in mercy, and sins thrown into the sea.

7.title: Who Is a God Like You?
7.overview:
Micah laments that he is like a man in an orchard after the harvest: the godly have perished and no one upright is left; all hunt each other, officials and judges take bribes and weave their schemes together, and the best of them is like a brier (vv. 1-4). Trust has collapsed to the point that neighbour, friend and even wife cannot be confided in, and a man's enemies are those of his own house (vv. 5-6). But as for Micah, he will look to the LORD and wait for the God of his salvation (v. 7).

God's people tell their enemy not to gloat: when they fall they will rise, and in darkness the LORD will be their light. They will bear the LORD's indignation because they have sinned, until he pleads their cause and brings them out to the light, and the enemy who asked "Where is the LORD your God?" will be shamed (vv. 8-10). A day is coming for rebuilding the walls, when people will come from Assyria, Egypt and as far as the Euphrates, though the earth is desolate because of its inhabitants' deeds (vv. 11-13).

Micah prays that God will shepherd his people with his staff and give them the old pastures, and God promises marvellous things as in the days of the exodus, before which the nations will cover their mouths and come trembling out of their strongholds (vv. 14-17). The book closes in wonder: who is a God like this, pardoning iniquity, delighting in steadfast love, treading iniquities underfoot, casting all our sins into the depths of the sea, keeping the oath sworn to Abraham and Jacob (vv. 18-20).
7.theology:
A society can decay until honesty is hard to find and corruption becomes a skilled, cooperative craft (vv. 2-4).

Sin finally reaches the family, and the gospel too can divide households — though for a very different reason (vv. 5-6; Matt 10:35-36).

The believer's response to a collapsing world is to look to the LORD, wait for him and expect to be heard (v. 7).

God's people fall, but they rise, because their rising depends on God's light rather than their strength (v. 8; Prov 24:16).

A believer may accept God's discipline as deserved and still be certain of vindication, for the Judge is also the advocate (v. 9; Rom 8:33-34).

God gathers the old enemies as pilgrims, even while the world reaps the fruit of its deeds (vv. 12-13; 4:1-2).

God forgives not reluctantly but gladly, because he delights in steadfast love (v. 18; Rom 3:25).

Forgiven sins are removed beyond recovery, and our security rests on God's sworn promise, fulfilled in Christ (vv. 19-20; Ps 103:12; Heb 8:12; Luke 1:72-73).

Old enemies arriving as pilgrims from every direction.
